Trail 3 Islamabad

The most famous and oldest hiking track of Islamabad is Trail 3. It starts from the Margalla Road in sector F-6/3. Due to steep hills, the trail is exhausting to some extent. The course leads to the point where it goes up to the Viewpoint and is about a 30–50 minutes track. After the Viewpoint it continues for another easy-going 45 – 60 minutes and reaches the Pir Sohawa, where there are two restaurants for food, *The Monal* and *La Montana*. In total, it is approximately a one-hour and thirty minute walk.[[95]](#cite_note-100)

Shah Allah Ditta village is a centuries-old village and a union council of the Islamabad Capital Authority. The village is named after a dervish who belonged to the Mughal era. It is estimated to be 650 years old approximately. It is also home to ancient caves that reflects the previous civilisations. The 2500-year-old Buddhist caves at the foot of Margalla Hills are located in west of Taxila, east of Islamabad and in the central area of Khanpur. A spring, a pond and a garden still exist near the Shah Allah Ditta Caves. There are some banyan trees in the garden, while all other fruit trees are gone. Main article: [Cornell Tech](/wiki/Cornell_Tech "Cornell Tech")

On 19 December 2011, a bid by a consortium of [Cornell University](/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") and Technion won a competition to establish a new high-tier applied science and engineering institution in New York City. The competition was established by New York City Mayor [Michael Bloomberg](/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg") in order to increase entrepreneurship and job growth in the city's technology sector. The winning bid consisted of a 2,100,000 square feet (200,000 m2) state-of-the-art tech campus, built on [Roosevelt Island](/wiki/Roosevelt_Island "Roosevelt Island"), which had its first phase completed by 2017, with a temporary off-site campus opening in 2013 at the [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") New York City headquarters building at [111 Eighth Avenue](/wiki/111_Eighth_Avenue "111 Eighth Avenue").[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23) The new school has been named the Jacobs Technion-Cornell Institute.[[23]](#cite_note-24) Its Founding Director was [Craig Gotsman](/wiki/Craig_Gotsman "Craig Gotsman"), Technion's Hewlett-Packard Professor of Computer Engineering.

In 2015, [AOL](/wiki/AOL "AOL") announced an investment of $5 million in a video research project at the institute.[[24]](#cite_note-25) Positive media coverage abounds,[[25]](#cite_note-26) as well as some small scale protests from the margins of political and environmental activism.[[26]](#cite_note-27)

Before its recognition as a planet, Uranus had been observed many times, but was generally misidentified as a star. It was apparently observed by [Hipparchus](/wiki/Hipparchus "Hipparchus"), who measured the positions of stars in 128 BC for his catalog that was later incorporated into [Ptolemy](/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy")'s *[Almagest](/wiki/Almagest "Almagest")*. The catalog gives the positions of four stars forming a quadrilateral in [Virgo](/wiki/Virgo_(constellation) "Virgo (constellation)"). One of the four stars does not exist, but Uranus was at that position in April of 128 BC.[[29]](#cite_note-35) The earliest definite sighting was in 1690, when [John Flamsteed](/wiki/John_Flamsteed "John Flamsteed") observed it at least six times, cataloguing it as 34 [Tauri](/wiki/Taurus_(constellation) "Taurus (constellation)"). [James Bradley](/wiki/James_Bradley "James Bradley") observed it three times, in 1748, 1750, and 1753. [Tobias Mayer](/wiki/Tobias_Mayer "Tobias Mayer") observed it once in 1756. The French astronomer [Pierre Charles Le Monnier](/wiki/Pierre_Charles_Le_Monnier "Pierre Charles Le Monnier") observed Uranus at least twelve times between 1750 and 1769, including on four consecutive nights.[[30]](#cite_note-36)

[William Herschel](/wiki/William_Herschel "William Herschel") observed Uranus on 13 March 1781 from the garden of his house at 19 New King Street in [Bath, Somerset](/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), England (now the [Herschel Museum of Astronomy](/wiki/Herschel_Museum_of_Astronomy "Herschel Museum of Astronomy")),[[31]](#cite_note-37) and initially reported it (on 26 April 1781) as a [comet](/wiki/Comet "Comet").[[32]](#cite_note-Ref-1-38) With a homemade 6.2-inch reflecting telescope, Herschel "engaged in a series of observations on the [parallax](/wiki/Parallax "Parallax") of the fixed stars."[[32]](#cite_note-Ref-1-38)[[33]](#cite_note-39)

After the first round of voting, Beijing held a significant lead over the other four candidates. Osaka received only six votes and was eliminated. The [1888 Philadelphia Phillies](/wiki/1888_Philadelphia_Quakers_season "1888 Philadelphia Quakers season") team

In [1883](/wiki/1883_Philadelphia_Quakers_season "1883 Philadelphia Quakers season"), sporting goods manufacturer [Al Reach](/wiki/Al_Reach "Al Reach"), a pioneering professional baseball player, and attorney [John Rogers](/wiki/John_Rogers_(baseball) "John Rogers (baseball)") won an expansion [National League](/wiki/National_League_(baseball) "National League (baseball)") franchise for Philadelphia, one of what is now known as the "Classic Eight" of the National League. They were awarded a spot in the league to replace the [Worcester baseball team](/wiki/Worcester_Worcesters "Worcester Worcesters"), a franchise that had folded in 1882. The new team was nicknamed the "Phillies" from the start, and immediately compiled a .173 [winning percentage](/wiki/Winning_percentage "Winning percentage"), which stands as the worst in franchise history. Although many sources (including the Phillies themselves) claim that Reach and Rogers bought the Brown Stockings and moved them to Philadelphia, all available evidence suggests this is not the case. Significantly, no players from Worcester[[18]](#cite_note-18) ended up with the 1883 Quakers.[[19]](#cite_note-19)
